# Section A — Which candidates work?

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA early specimen · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
A set of five cards each have a letter printed on their front and a number printed on their back, as follows:

| | Card A | Card B | Card C | Card D | Card E |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| **Fronts** | A | B | C | D | E |
| **Backs** | 3 | 4 | 1 | 7 | 8 |

Which one of the five cards (A, B, C, D or E) provides a **counterexample** to the following statement?

> *Every card that has a vowel on its front has an even number on its back.*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**Card A.**

**Step 1 — write it as "if … then".** For every card: if it has a vowel on its front, then it has an even number on
its back.

**Step 2 — say what a counterexample must look like.** The hypothesis must be true and the conclusion false, so
we need a vowel on the front **and** an odd number on the back.

**Step 3 — check the cards.** Only A and E have vowels on the front.

- Card A has $3$ on the back, which is odd. This breaks the statement.
- Card E has $8$ on the back, which is even. The statement holds for this card.

**Why not the others?** B, C and D have consonants on the front, so the statement says nothing about them. Cards C
and D have odd backs, which is what makes them tempting, but the hypothesis fails.
:::

## Question 2 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement about the positive integer $n$:

> if $n$ is prime, then $n^2+2$ is not prime

Which of the following is a counterexample to this statement?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $n=2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $n=3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $n=4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C — II only.**

A counterexample needs $n$ prime **and** $n^2+2$ prime.

| $n$ | $n$ prime? | $n^2+2$ | $n^2+2$ prime? | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $2$ | yes | $6$ | no | no: the statement holds here |
| $3$ | yes | $11$ | **yes** | **yes** |
| $4$ | **no** | $18$ | no | no: the hypothesis fails |

**Why $n=4$ is not one.** The statement only talks about prime $n$. It makes no claim about $4$.
:::

---

## Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following claim about positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$:

> if $a$ is a factor of $bc$, then $a$ is a factor of $b$ or $a$ is a factor of $c$

Which of the following provide(s) a counterexample to this claim?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $a=5,\ b=10,\ c=20$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $a=8,\ b=4,\ c=4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $a=6,\ b=7,\ c=12$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C — II only.**

A counterexample needs $a$ to divide $bc$, but $a$ to divide **neither** $b$ nor $c$. Negating the "or" is what makes
it "neither".

| | $bc$ | $a$ divides $bc$? | $a$ divides $b$? | $a$ divides $c$? | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | $200$ | yes | yes | yes | no |
| **II** | $16$ | yes | no | no | **yes** |
| **III** | $84$ | yes | no | yes | no |

**The idea behind it.** The factor $8=2^3$ can be shared out between $b$ and $c$, with some powers of $2$ in each. The
claim does hold when $a$ is prime, which is why it looks believable.
:::

## Question 4 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement:

> Every positive integer $N$ that is greater than $6$ can be written as the sum of two non-prime integers that are
> greater than $1$.

Which of the following is/are counterexample(s) to this statement?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $N=5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $N=7$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $N=9$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**G — II and III only.**

A counterexample is an $N$ greater than $6$ that **cannot** be written this way. The non-primes greater than $1$ begin
$4,6,8,9,\dots$

- **$N=5$** is not greater than $6$, so the statement says nothing about it. Not a counterexample.
- **$N=7$:** the splits into numbers greater than $1$ are $2+5$ and $3+4$. Each contains a prime, so $7$ cannot be
  written this way. Counterexample.
- **$N=9$:** the splits are $2+7$, $3+6$ and $4+5$. Each contains a prime, so $9$ cannot be written this way.
  Counterexample.

**Quick check on $9$.** The smallest possible sum is $4+4=8$, and the next is $4+6=10$. So $9$ is skipped.
:::

## Question 5 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following conjecture:

> If $N$ is a positive integer that consists of the digit $1$ followed by an odd number of $0$ digits and then a final
> digit $1$, then $N$ is a prime number.

Here are three numbers:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $N=101$ (which is a prime number)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $N=1001$ (which equals $7\times11\times13$)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $N=10001$ (which equals $73\times137$)

Which of these provide(s) a counterexample to the conjecture?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D — III only.**

A counterexample must have the right form (an **odd** number of zeros) **and** be not prime.

| $N$ | zeros | right form? | prime? | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $101$ | $1$ | yes | yes | no: the conjecture holds here |
| $1001$ | $2$ | **no** | no | no: the hypothesis fails |
| $10001$ | $3$ | yes | **no** | **yes** |

**The trap is $1001$.** It is composite, and the question even shows the factors, but it has an even number of zeros.
The conjecture never mentioned it.
:::

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2016 · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the statement:

> $(*)$ A whole number $n$ is prime if it is $1$ less or $5$ less than a multiple of $6$.

How many counterexamples to $(*)$ are there in the range $0<n<50$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $6$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C — four.**

**Step 1 — rewrite the word "if".** "$A$ is prime **if** $B$" means "if $B$, then $A$ is prime". So:

> if $n$ is $1$ less or $5$ less than a multiple of $6$, then $n$ is prime.

**Step 2 — list the numbers fitting the hypothesis.** Being $1$ less than a multiple of $6$ gives
$5,11,17,23,29,35,41,47$. Being $5$ less gives $1,7,13,19,25,31,37,43,49$.

**Step 3 — pick out the ones that are not prime.**
$$1,\quad 25=5^2,\quad 35=5\times7,\quad 49=7^2 .$$

That is four counterexamples.

**The one people miss is $n=1$.** It is $5$ less than $6$, and $1$ is not prime.
:::

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following three statements:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**1** &nbsp; $10p^2+1$ and $10p^2-1$ are both prime when $p$ is an odd prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**2** &nbsp; Every prime greater than $5$ is of the form $6n+1$ for some integer $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3** &nbsp; No multiple of $7$ greater than $7$ is prime.

The result $91=7\times13$ can be used to provide a counterexample to which of the above statements?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** **1** only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** **2** only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** **3** only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** **1** and **2** only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** **1** and **3** only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** **2** and **3** only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** **1**, **2** and **3**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B — statement 1 only.**

The fact tells us $91$ is **not prime**, and that it is a multiple of $7$ and of $13$. Test it against each statement.

**Statement 1.** Take the odd prime $p=3$. Then $10p^2+1=91$, which is not prime. The hypothesis holds and the
conclusion fails, so this is a counterexample.

**Statement 2.** This statement is about primes, and $91$ is not prime, so the fact says nothing. *(The statement is
false, because $11=6\times2-1$, but $91$ is not what shows it.)*

**Statement 3.** $91$ is a multiple of $7$ greater than $7$, and it is not prime. That **agrees** with the statement.
Agreeing with a statement is the opposite of breaking it. In fact statement 3 is true, so it has no counterexample.
:::

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock B · P2 Q1</span>

::: {.question}
It is a fact that
$$1729=1^3+12^3=9^3+10^3=7\times13\times19 .$$

Consider the following four statements.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** Every positive integer that can be written as a sum of two positive cubes in two different ways is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** If a prime $p>5$ can be written as $p=a^3+b^3$ for some positive integers $a,b$, then $p$ has remainder of $1$ when divided by $6$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** No product of three distinct odd primes is one more than a perfect cube.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** Every positive integer of the form $a^3+b^3$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers, has prime factors all of which are at least $3$.

The fact above can be used to provide a counterexample to which of these statements?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** 1 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** 1 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** 2 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** 1, 2 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** 1, 3 and 4 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** 1, 2, 3 and 4
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D — 1 and 3 only.**

**Statement 1.** $1729$ is a sum of two positive cubes in two different ways, and $1729=7\times13\times19$ is not prime.
Hypothesis true, conclusion false, so this is a counterexample.

**Statement 2.** This is about primes, and $1729$ is not prime. The fact is outside the hypothesis.

**Statement 3.** $1729$ is a product of three distinct odd primes. Also $1729=1^3+12^3$, so
$$1729=12^3+1,$$
which is one more than a perfect cube. The statement says this never happens, so this is a counterexample. *Rewriting
$1^3+12^3$ as $12^3+1$ is the step to spot.*

**Statement 4.** $1729$ is of the form $a^3+b^3$, and its prime factors $7,13,19$ are all at least $3$. It **agrees**
with the statement, so it is not a counterexample.
:::

# Section B — Prove it or break it

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise P, Q1</span>

::: {.question}
What would constitute a counterexample to a statement of the form:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**a.** &nbsp; $A$ and $B$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**b.** &nbsp; $A$ or $B$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**c.** &nbsp; $A$ only if $B$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**d.** &nbsp; $A$ iff $B$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

A counterexample is a case that makes the statement false, so ask when each form is false.

**a.** "$A$ and $B$" needs both, so it fails as soon as **at least one of $A$, $B$ is false**.

**b.** "$A$ or $B$" needs just one, so it fails only when **$A$ and $B$ are both false**.

**c.** "$A$ only if $B$" means "if $A$ then $B$". It fails when **$A$ is true and $B$ is false**.

**d.** "$A$ iff $B$" says the two always match. It fails when **one is true and the other is false**, in either order.
:::

---

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise P, Q2</span>

::: {.question}
Find a counterexample, if one exists, to each of the following:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**a.** &nbsp; all prime numbers are odd and greater than $4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**b.** &nbsp; all prime numbers are odd or greater than $37$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**c.** &nbsp; $x$ is prime if and only if $x$ is odd

&nbsp;&nbsp;**d.** &nbsp; $x$ is odd only if $x$ is prime

&nbsp;&nbsp;**e.** &nbsp; $x$ is prime only if $x$ is odd

&nbsp;&nbsp;**f.** &nbsp; for all positive odd integers $x$: $x$ is prime or $x$ is divisible by some integer $k<x$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

Use the answers to Question 9 in each part.

**a.** We need a prime that is even **or** not greater than $4$. Both $2$ and $3$ work. Note that $3$ is odd, but it is
not greater than $4$.

**b.** We need a prime that is even **and** not greater than $37$. The only even prime is $2$, and it qualifies. So $2$
is the only counterexample.

**c.** We need a number that is one but not the other: $2$ is prime and not odd, and $9$ is odd and not prime.

**d.** "If $x$ is odd, then $x$ is prime". We need an odd non-prime, such as $9$.

**e.** "If $x$ is prime, then $x$ is odd". We need an even prime, so $x=2$.

**f.** No counterexample exists, if we read "some integer $k$" literally. The only awkward case is $x=1$, which is
odd and not prime. If $k$ must be positive, then no $k<1$ exists, so $x=1$ **would** be a counterexample. But the
statement says *integer*, and $k=-1$ satisfies $k<1$ and divides $1$. In fact $k=-1$ divides every integer, so the
statement holds for every $x$.

*Parts (d) and (e) use the same two words in opposite orders, and they need different counterexamples.*
:::

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA early specimen · P2 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
For any real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ where $a\ge b$, consider these three statements:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**1** &nbsp; $-b\ge-a$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**2** &nbsp; $a^2+b^2\ge2ab$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3** &nbsp; $ac\ge bc$

Which of the statements 1, 2, and 3 **must** be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** 1 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** 1 and 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** 1 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** 2 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** 1, 2 and 3
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E — 1 and 2 only.**

**Statement 1 — prove it.** Multiply $a\ge b$ by $-1$. Multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality, so
$-a\le-b$, which is the same as $-b\ge-a$. True.

**Statement 2 — prove it.** Rearrange to $a^2-2ab+b^2\ge0$, which is
$$(a-b)^2\ge0 .$$
A square is never negative, so this is true. The condition $a\ge b$ is not even needed.

**Statement 3 — break it.** The sign of $c$ is not given. Take $a=2$, $b=1$, $c=-1$. Then $a\ge b$ holds, but $ac=-2$
and $bc=-1$, and $-2\ge-1$ is false.
:::

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q14</span>

::: {.question}
Suppose that $n$ is an integer such that $n^3$ is divisible by $5$.

Which of the following statements are necessarily true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $5$ is a factor of $n$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $n^3$ is divisible by $125$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; If $k$ is a multiple of $5$ which divides $n^3$, then $\dfrac{n^3}{k}$ is a multiple of $5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E — I and II only.**

**I — prove it.** $n^3=n\times n\times n$. Since $5$ is prime and divides this product, it must divide one of the factors,
and each factor is $n$. So $5$ divides $n$.

**II — prove it.** By I, write $n=5m$ for an integer $m$. Then $n^3=125m^3$, which is divisible by $125$.

**III — break it.** Take $n=10$, so $n^3=1000=5^3\times2^3$. Take $k=125$, which is a multiple of $5$ dividing $1000$. Then
$$\frac{n^3}{k}=\frac{1000}{125}=8,$$
which is not a multiple of $5$.

**Why III fails.** $n^3$ contains at least three factors of $5$, and $k$ can use all of them, leaving none behind.
:::

## Question 13 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
An arithmetic series has $n$ terms, all of which are integers.

The sum of the series is $20$.

Which of the following statements must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; The first term of the series is even.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $n$ is even.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; The common difference is even.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A — none of them.**

Each statement falls to one small series, so we just need to find them.

**Step 1 — set up.** With first term $a$ and common difference $d$,
$$\tfrac12n\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr)=20,\quad\text{so}\quad n\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr)=40 .$$
So $n$ must be a factor of $40$, which tells us which lengths to try.

**Step 2 — break each statement.**

- **I:** take $n=2$, with $9+11=20$. The first term is $9$, which is odd.
- **II:** take $n=5$, with $2+3+4+5+6=20$. Here $n$ is odd.
- **III:** the same series $2+3+4+5+6$ has $d=1$, which is odd.

One series, $9+11$, breaks I and another, $2+3+4+5+6$, breaks II and III.
:::

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">MAT 2016 · Q1J</span>

::: {.question}
Let $n>1$ be an integer. Let $\Pi(n)$ denote the number of distinct prime factors of $n$ and let $x(n)$ denote the final
digit of $n$. For example, $\Pi(8)=1$ and $\Pi(6)=2$. Which of the following statements is **false**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** If $\Pi(n)=1$, there are some values of $x(n)$ that mean $n$ cannot be prime,

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** If $\Pi(n)=1$, there are some values of $x(n)$ that mean $n$ must be prime,

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** If $\Pi(n)=1$, there are values of $x(n)$ which are impossible,

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** If $\Pi(n)+x(n)=2$, we cannot tell if $n$ is prime,

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(e)** If $\Pi(n)=2$, all values of $x(n)$ are possible.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(b).**

$\Pi(n)=1$ means $n$ is a power of a single prime, such as $7$, $8$ or $81$.

**(a) is true.** Take $x(n)=4$, as in $n=4$. A number ending in $4$ is even and bigger than $2$, so it cannot be prime.

**(b) is false.** Go through the final digits a prime can have. Each also occurs on a prime power that is not prime:

| final digit | prime | non-prime power of a prime |
|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $11$ | $81=3^4$ |
| $2$ | $2$ | $32=2^5$ |
| $3$ | $3$ | $243=3^5$ |
| $5$ | $5$ | $25=5^2$ |
| $7$ | $7$ | $27=3^3$ |
| $9$ | $19$ | $9=3^2$ |

No final digit forces $n$ to be prime.

**(c) is true.** $x(n)=0$ is impossible, because such an $n$ is divisible by both $2$ and $5$, which gives $\Pi(n)\ge2$.

**(d) is true.** $\Pi(n)+x(n)=2$ allows $\Pi(n)=1,\ x(n)=1$. Then $n=11$ is prime but $n=81$ is not, so we cannot tell.

**(e) is true.** Each digit occurs: $10,21,12,33,14,15,6,57,18,39$ all have exactly two distinct prime factors.
:::

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">MAT 2025 · Q26Y(ii)</span>

::: {.question}
Linear polynomials are functions of the form $a+bx$ with $a$ and $b$ real numbers.

Given two linear polynomials, we define an operation $\cdot$ as follows. To calculate $f(x)\cdot g(x)$, we multiply the
polynomials as normal, but we ignore any $x^2$ term.

For example, $(1-2x)\cdot(3-5x)=3-11x$, because we are ignoring the $10x^2$ term.

A strictly increasing linear function $f(x)$ has the property that if $y>x$ then $f(y)>f(x)$.

A student claims that if $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are both strictly increasing linear functions then so is $f(x)\cdot g(x)$. Is
the student correct? If so, prove the student's claim. Otherwise, find a counterexample.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**The student is not correct.**

**Step 1 — work out the rule.** Multiplying and ignoring the $x^2$ term gives
$$(a+bx)\cdot(c+dx)=ac+(ad+bc)x .$$
A linear function is strictly increasing exactly when its $x$ coefficient is positive. So $f$ and $g$ being increasing
means $b>0$ and $d>0$, and we want $ad+bc\le0$.

**Step 2 — choose constants to make $ad+bc$ negative.** Since $b$ and $d$ are positive, a negative constant term can do
it. Take $f(x)=1+x$ and $g(x)=-2+x$. Both have $x$ coefficient $1$, so both are strictly increasing. Then
$$(1+x)\cdot(-2+x)=-2+(1\times1+1\times(-2))x=-2-x .$$

**Step 3 — check.** $-2-x$ has $x$ coefficient $-1$, so it is decreasing, and the claim fails.
:::

---

## Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2016 · P2 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
Consider this statement about a function $\mathrm{f}(x)$:

> $(*)$ If $\bigl(\mathrm{f}(x)\bigr)^2\le1$ for all $-1\le x\le1$ then $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\bigl(\mathrm{f}(x)\bigr)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\le\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm{f}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$

Which one of the following functions provides a **counterexample** to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\mathrm{f}(x)=x+\dfrac12$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $\mathrm{f}(x)=x-\dfrac12$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $\mathrm{f}(x)=x+x^3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $\mathrm{f}(x)=x-x^3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $\mathrm{f}(x)=x^2+x^4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $\mathrm{f}(x)=x^2-x^4$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.**

**Step 1 — test the hypothesis first, because it is cheap.**

- **A:** $\mathrm{f}(1)=\tfrac32$, so $\mathrm{f}(1)^2>1$. Out.
- **B:** $\mathrm{f}(-1)=-\tfrac32$, so $\mathrm{f}(-1)^2>1$. Out.
- **C:** $\mathrm{f}(1)=2$. Out.
- **E:** $\mathrm{f}(1)=2$. Out.

That leaves D and F.

**Step 2 — check that D and F satisfy the hypothesis.**

For **D**, $\mathrm{f}(x)=x-x^3$ has $\mathrm{f}'(x)=1-3x^2$, so its stationary points are at $x=\pm\tfrac1{\sqrt3}$, where
$\lvert \mathrm{f}\rvert=\tfrac{2}{3\sqrt3}<1$. Also $\mathrm{f}(\pm1)=0$. So $\mathrm{f}(x)^2\le1$ on the whole interval.

For **F**, $\mathrm{f}(x)=x^2-x^4$ has maximum value $\tfrac14$ on the interval and is never negative there.

**Step 3 — test the conclusion.**

For **D**, $\mathrm{f}$ is an odd function, so $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm{f}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=0$. The integral of $\mathrm{f}^2$ is positive,
because a square is never negative and $\mathrm{f}$ is not always zero. Exactly,
$$\int_{-1}^{1}(x-x^3)^2\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{16}{105}>0 .$$
So the conclusion fails, and **D is the counterexample**.

For **F**, $0\le\mathrm{f}(x)<1$ gives $\mathrm{f}(x)^2\le\mathrm{f}(x)$ everywhere, so the conclusion holds.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "y = x − x³ on [−1, 1]: it stays within ±1, and the two lobes cancel, so its integral is 0."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x = np.linspace(-1, 1, 400); y = x - x**3
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 3.2))
ax.fill_between(x, y, 0, where=(y > 0), color='#1f77b4', alpha=0.18)
ax.fill_between(x, y, 0, where=(y < 0), color='#d62728', alpha=0.18)
ax.plot(x, y, color='#1f77b4', lw=2.2, label=r'$y=x-x^{3}$')
ax.axhline(0, color='0.55', lw=0.9); ax.axvline(0, color='0.55', lw=0.9)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y'); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 0.6)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='upper right')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

---

## Question 17 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
It is given that $\mathrm{f}(x)=x^3+3qx^2+2$, where $q$ is a real constant.

The equation $\mathrm{f}(x)=0$ has $3$ distinct real roots.

Which of the following statements is/are necessarily true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; The equation $\mathrm{f}(x)+1=0$ has $3$ distinct real roots.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; The equation $\mathrm{f}(x+1)=0$ has $3$ distinct real roots.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; The equation $\mathrm{f}(-x)-1=0$ has $3$ distinct real roots.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**G — II and III only.**

**Step 1 — find the turning points.** $\mathrm{f}'(x)=3x^2+6qx=3x(x+2q)$, so the stationary points are at $x=0$ and $x=-2q$:
$$(0,\ 2)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(-2q,\ 2+4q^3).$$

**Step 2 — use the hypothesis.** Three distinct roots means the turning points lie on opposite sides of the $x$-axis.
The first is at height $2>0$, so the second must be below the axis:
$$2+4q^3<0 .$$

**II — prove it.** $y=\mathrm{f}(x+1)$ is $y=\mathrm{f}(x)$ moved $1$ left. Sliding sideways does not change the number of crossings. True.

**III — prove it.** Put $t=-x$. Then $\mathrm{f}(-x)-1=0$ is the same as $\mathrm{f}(t)=1$, and each root $t$ gives one root $x$.
The line $y=1$ lies strictly between the two turning-point heights, since $2+4q^3<0<1<2$. So it crosses the cubic three
times. True.

**I — break it.** $\mathrm{f}(x)+1=0$ means $\mathrm{f}(x)=-1$, so it has three roots only if the lower turning point is below
$-1$. The hypothesis only puts it below $0$. Take $q=-0.8$, so $2+4q^3=-0.048$. That is below $0$, so $\mathrm{f}(x)=0$ has three
roots, but it is above $-1$, so $\mathrm{f}(x)+1=0$ has only one root.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "q = −0.8: y = f(x) crosses the x-axis three times, because the lower turning point is just below it."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
q = -0.8; x = np.linspace(-1.2, 2.8, 500); f = x**3 + 3*q*x**2 + 2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 3.2))
ax.plot(x, f, color='#1f77b4', lw=2.2, label=r'$y=f(x)$')
ax.axhline(0, color='0.55', lw=0.9); ax.axvline(0, color='0.55', lw=0.9)
ax.plot([0, 1.6], [2, 2+4*q**3], 'o', color='#d62728', zorder=5)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y'); ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 4); ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='upper left')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "q = −0.8: y = f(x) + 1 is the same curve moved up 1. The lower turning point is now above the axis, so there is only one root."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
q = -0.8; x = np.linspace(-1.2, 2.8, 500); f = x**3 + 3*q*x**2 + 3
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 3.2))
ax.plot(x, f, color='#1f77b4', lw=2.2, label=r'$y=f(x)+1$')
ax.axhline(0, color='0.55', lw=0.9); ax.axvline(0, color='0.55', lw=0.9)
ax.plot([0, 1.6], [3, 3+4*q**3], 'o', color='#d62728', zorder=5)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y'); ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 4); ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='upper left')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

# Section C — Judging a proof

## Question 18 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise O, Q2</span>

::: {.question}
Can you adapt the proof that $\sqrt2$ is irrational to show that $\sqrt p$ is irrational for all prime $p$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**Yes.**

**Step 1 — assume the opposite.** Suppose $\sqrt p=\dfrac ab$, with $a,b$ positive integers and the fraction in lowest terms.

**Step 2 — square.** $a^2=pb^2$, so $p$ divides $a^2=a\times a$.

**Step 3 — use that $p$ is prime.** A prime dividing a product must divide one of the factors, so $p$ divides $a$. Write
$a=pc$.

**Step 4 — substitute.** $p^2c^2=pb^2$, so $b^2=pc^2$. Then $p$ divides $b^2$, and in the same way $p$ divides $b$.

**Step 5 — the contradiction.** $p$ divides both $a$ and $b$, but $\dfrac ab$ was in lowest terms. So $\sqrt p$ is irrational.

*Step 3 is the only place primality is used. For $p=9$ it fails, since $9$ can divide $a^2$ without dividing $a$ (take $a=3$).*
:::

---

## Question 19 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to prove the following claim:

> For every positive integer $n$, if $n^2+2$ is prime, then $n$ is a multiple of $3$.

The student's argument is given line by line below.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I.** Suppose $n$ is a positive integer such that $n^2+2$ is prime, but $n$ is not a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II.** Then the remainder of $n$ on division by $3$ is $1$ or $2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III.** In either case, $n^2$ leaves remainder $1$ when divided by $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV.** Therefore $n^2+2$ leaves remainder $0$ when divided by $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V.** So $3$ divides $n^2+2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI.** Hence $n^2+2=3k$ for some integer $k$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VII.** It follows that $n^2+2$ is composite and not prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VIII.** This contradicts the assumption in (I) that $n^2+2$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IX.** Therefore $n$ is a multiple of $3$.

Which one of the following statements about the argument is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The argument is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The first error in the argument is on line I.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The first error in the argument is on line II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The first error in the argument is on line III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The first error in the argument is on line IV.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** The first error in the argument is on line V.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** The first error in the argument is on line VI.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** The first error in the argument is on line VII.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** The first error in the argument is on line VIII.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**J** The first error in the argument is on line IX.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**H — line VII.**

**Lines I–VI are all correct.** Line I is the right opening for a contradiction on an "if … then": assume the hypothesis and
deny the conclusion. For lines II–III, $1^2=1$ and $2^2=4$ both leave remainder $1$. Lines IV–VI follow directly.

**Line VII is the error.** $n^2+2=3k$ is composite only if $k>1$. If $k=1$, the number is $3$ itself, and $3$ is prime.

**This is more than a gap, because the claim is false.** Take $n=1$. Then $n^2+2=3$ is prime, and $1$ is not a multiple of $3$. That
is a counterexample.

**The habit.** "A multiple of $3$ is not prime" has one exception, and it is $3$. Whenever a proof says "divisible by $p$, so not
prime", ask whether the number could be $p$ itself.
:::

---

## Question 20 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
In this question, $n$ is an integer greater than $1$.

**Statement:** If $n$ does not divide $k!$ for any positive integer $k$ with $k<n$, then $n$ is prime.

The following is an attempted proof of the statement:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** Assume $n$ does not divide $k!$ for any positive integer $k$ with $k<n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Suppose for contradiction that $n$ is composite, so $n=ab$ for some integers $a,b$ with $1<a\le b<n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** Case 1: $a<b$. Then $a$ and $b$ are distinct integers, each in the set $\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** Therefore $a$ and $b$ both appear as factors in the product $(n-1)!=1\cdot2\cdots(n-1)$, so $ab=n$ divides $(n-1)!$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(5)** Case 2: $a=b$, so $n=a^2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(6)** Since $a\ge2$, the integers $a$ and $2a$ both satisfy $a\ge2$ and $2a\ge4$, so they are positive integers.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(7)** Since $a\ge2$, we have $a<a^2=n$ and $2a<a^2=n$, so $a$ and $2a$ are distinct integers in the set $\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(8)** Therefore $a$ and $2a$ both appear as factors in $(n-1)!$, so $a\cdot2a=2a^2=2n$ divides $(n-1)!$, and in particular $n$ divides $(n-1)!$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(9)** In both cases $n$ divides $(n-1)!$, contradicting the assumption in line 1. Hence $n$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** First mistake appears in line 1 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** First mistake appears in line 2 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** First mistake appears in line 3 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** First mistake appears in line 4 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** First mistake appears in line 5 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** First mistake appears in line 6 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** First mistake appears in line 7 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** The proof is valid and the statement is true.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**G — line 7, and the statement is false.**

**Lines 1–2** set up the contradiction correctly.

**Case 1 (lines 3–4) is fine.** $a$ and $b$ are different numbers below $n$, so they are separate factors of $(n-1)!$.

**Lines 5–6 are fine**, if unexciting.

**Line 7 is the mistake.** $2a<a^2$ means $2<a$, so it needs $a\ge3$. When $a=2$, we get $2a=4=a^2=n$, which is not below $n$.

**The statement really does fail there.** Take $n=4=2\times2$. Then $1!=1$, $2!=2$ and $3!=6$, and $4$ divides none of them, so the
hypothesis holds. But $4$ is not prime. So $n=4$ is a counterexample, and the proof's gap is exactly at this one value.

**The habit.** When a proof by cases uses an inequality like "since $a\ge2$", test the smallest allowed value.
:::
